name: borsel
author: rule-family designer (dice)
description: DICE RULE-FAMILY class (docs/RULE_FAMILIES.md; brainstorm in challenges/lab/NOTES_rules_dice.md). CLUE = 2 or 3 example rolls of k dice (k=3, 4 or 5, fixed within a clue), pips space-separated, one roll per line, dice in RANDOM order. ANSWER = one more roll of k dice obeying the hidden rule and not a re-ordering of an example (the scorer compares sorted multisets, so copying an example, shuffled or not, scores 0). UNIVERSE U (11 templates, 26-27 concrete rules depending on k; d = sorted roll, S = total, M = biggest, m = smallest): (0) S == n for n in {3k-2, 3k, 3k+2, 3k+4}; (1) S > 4k+2; (2) S < 3k-2; (3) M == 3 or 4; (4) m == 3 or 4; (5) exactly two dice show v, v in 1..6; (6) exactly i different numbers, i in 1..min(k-2,2); (7) the two biggest add up to k+3 or k+4; (8) the two smallest add up to 10-k or 11-k; (9) M == 2*m; (10) M+m == n for n in {4,5,9,10}. Every rule is a one-breath kid sentence and every parameter value was picked so the rule's probability under a uniform roll is 0.02-0.17 (mean 0.10) - that number is what a player who answers at random scores. U is an ANTICHAIN (verified by brute force over all multisets for k=3,4,5): no rule contains another, otherwise positive examples could never separate them. That is why there is only one 'more than' and one 'less than' threshold, why 'multiple of y' and 'exactly c dice are odd' are absent, and why the max/min grids stop at 3 and 4. GENERATE draws the TEMPLATE uniformly first, then a parameter (so no template is rare merely for having fewer parameters), then searches for a MINIMAL identifying example set: 40 random triples for a 3-set whose three examples together leave exactly one rule of U alive while no two of them do, else a minimal pair. Measured over 500 clues: 43% three examples, 57% two; templates 31-56 occurrences each; mean 0.066 ms; clue <= 29 chars; answer <= 9 chars. DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED (never the rule, often consistent with the examples - the trap the class teaches; 'fits' = consistent with all examples, 'scores' = rate of a player who always answers with an instance of it): 'every die is at least m' fits 100% scores 23%; 'no die is bigger than m' fits 100% scores 20%; 'the total is odd/even' 43%/12%; 'exactly c of the dice are odd' 20%/10%; 'two of the dice add up to seven' 18%/8%; 'there is a six' 12%/7%; 'the dice are in increasing order' 8%/10%; 'all odd / all even' 6%/1%; 'three of them are in a row' 3%/13%; 'all the dice are different' 1%/4%. The class only ever makes TIGHT statements (exactly n, exactly two, the biggest IS 4) and never loose ones (at least, at most, contains); the loose cousins of its own templates are the two 100%-consistent traps. WITNESSES over 500 fresh clues: copy an example verbatim 0%; copy an example with one die changed 28% (the foothold); a random roll 10%; 'answer with the same total as example 1' 35% (the strongest cheap template); 'biggest die = biggest pip seen' 24%; a player who knows U but picks the wrong survivor 19%; a player who has mapped all of U 100%; all but the two rarest templates 87%; the 3 most common templates 53%; the 5 most common 62%; one template only 38%. SOLVE enumerates the rolls satisfying the unique survivor, drops the examples and returns a uniformly random one in random dice order (never canonical, never minimal). SCORE is 653 chars and needs max_score_code_chars = 1024 (the raise RULE_FAMILIES.md sec.4 allows for this paradigm).

def U_of(k):
    """The universe: 11 one-breath rules about a roll of k dice, 26-27 concrete rules."""
    return ([(0, n) for n in (3*k-2, 3*k, 3*k+2, 3*k+4)]     # the dice add up to exactly n
        + [(1, 4*k+2)]                                       # ... add up to more than n
        + [(2, 3*k-2)]                                       # ... add up to less than n
        + [(3, m) for m in (3, 4)]                           # the biggest die is m
        + [(4, m) for m in (3, 4)]                           # the smallest die is m
        + [(5, v) for v in range(1, 7)]                      # exactly two of the dice show v
        + [(6, i) for i in range(1, min(k-1, 3))]            # exactly i different numbers
        + [(7, s) for s in (k+3, k+4)]                       # the two biggest add up to s
        + [(8, s) for s in (10-k, 11-k)]                     # the two smallest add up to s
        + [(9, 0)]                                           # the biggest is double the smallest
        + [(10, n) for n in (4, 5, 9, 10)])                  # biggest + smallest = n

def P(r, d):
    """d is a SORTED tuple of k pips (1..6)."""
    t, q = r
    S = sum(d)
    M = d[-1]
    m = d[0]
    return [S == q, S > q, S < q, M == q, m == q, d.count(q) == 2, len(set(d)) == q,
            M+d[-2] == q, m+d[1] == q, M == 2*m, M+m == q][t]

CACHE = {}

def tables(k):
    if k in CACHE:
        return CACHE[k]
    U = U_of(k)
    M = list(itertools.combinations_with_replacement(range(1, 7), k))
    masks = []
    for d in M:
        b = 0
        for j, r in enumerate(U):
            if P(r, d):
                b |= 1 << j
        masks.append(b)
    sat = [[i for i, b in enumerate(masks) if b >> j & 1] for j in range(len(U))]
    CACHE[k] = (U, M, masks, sat)
    return CACHE[k]

def generate(seed):
    r = random.Random(seed)
    for _ in range(400):
        k = r.choice((3, 4, 4, 5, 5))
        U, M, masks, sat = tables(k)
        t = r.randrange(11)                        # template first, so no template is rare
        js = [j for j, u in enumerate(U) if u[0] == t]
        if not js:
            continue
        j = r.choice(js)
        A = sat[j]
        if len(A) < 5:
            continue
        best = None
        # a MINIMAL identifying set of 3 examples: all three together leave exactly one
        # rule of U alive, and no two of them do
        for _t in range(40):
            T = r.sample(A, 3)
            if (masks[T[0]] & masks[T[1]] & masks[T[2]]).bit_count() != 1:
                continue
            if (masks[T[0]] & masks[T[1]]).bit_count() == 1:
                continue
            if (masks[T[0]] & masks[T[2]]).bit_count() == 1:
                continue
            if (masks[T[1]] & masks[T[2]]).bit_count() == 1:
                continue
            best = T
            break
        if best is None:                           # else a minimal pair
            for _t in range(40):
                T = r.sample(A, 2)
                if (masks[T[0]] & masks[T[1]]).bit_count() == 1 and masks[T[0]].bit_count() > 1 and masks[T[1]].bit_count() > 1:
                    best = T
                    break
        if best is None or len(A) < len(best) + 2:
            continue
        lines = []
        for i in best:
            d = list(M[i])
            r.shuffle(d)
            lines.append(" ".join(map(str, d)))
        return "\n".join(lines)
    return "1 1 2\n2 2 1"

def U_of(k):
    return ([(0, n) for n in (3*k-2, 3*k, 3*k+2, 3*k+4)]
        + [(1, 4*k+2), (2, 3*k-2), (9, 0)]
        + [(3, m) for m in (3, 4)]
        + [(4, m) for m in (3, 4)]
        + [(5, v) for v in range(1, 7)]
        + [(6, i) for i in range(1, min(k-1, 3))]
        + [(7, s) for s in (k+3, k+4)]
        + [(8, s) for s in (10-k, 11-k)]
        + [(10, n) for n in (4, 5, 9, 10)])

def P(r, d):
    t, q = r
    S = sum(d)
    M = d[-1]
    m = d[0]
    return [S == q, S > q, S < q, M == q, m == q, d.count(q) == 2, len(set(d)) == q,
            M+d[-2] == q, m+d[1] == q, M == 2*m, M+m == q][t]

def solve(clue):
    E = [tuple(sorted(int(x) for x in l.split())) for l in clue.strip().split("\n")]
    k = len(E[0])
    V = [r for r in U_of(k) if all(P(r, e) for e in E)]
    ok = [d for d in itertools.combinations_with_replacement(range(1, 7), k)
          if P(V[0], d) and d not in E]
    r = random.Random(clue)
    d = list(r.choice(ok))      # a random valid roll, never a canonical one
    r.shuffle(d)                # in random dice order, exactly like the examples
    return " ".join(map(str, d))
